reviews.text: As a major motion picture, CA:BNW is a non-entity, deceptively non-sensical in its spackled, empty-headed narrative. It's unclear what the film is attempting to say other than suggesting the necessity of embracing one's own strengths AND weaknesses.
Mackie delivers a charismatic performance ... [But] the story sputters where it should soar.
There’s some action in the film that’s frankly unforgettable, with a creative spin on a character we’ve seen before.

Cap IV is a... hammer, good for little more than hitting things until all the things are hit. It is not about finesse, or sculpting something beautiful. It just hits, in unsubtle but effective ways, until all the nails have been hammered home.

It is pretty entertaining – and also nice to see Mackie and Ford with roles they seem to enjoy – it’s also dangerously close in quality to being a direct to streaming viewing rather than a big family IMAX outing.
There's no excuse for this to be this poorly executed.
Brave New World's kinetic moments of spectacle aren’t enough to make the movie feel like it has anything substantive to say about who Sam is or how his becoming Captain America changes the world

A plot without something to say is directionless, and characters without a point of view are doomed to remain one-dimensional. The simple fact is, you can’t make a political thriller devoid of political commentary...

Another frustratingly mediocre MCU film. It has its high points, but all throughout the runtime you're constantly reminded of better films in the franchise. And your brain keeps coming up with a better version of this film than the one they delivered.
Captain America: Brave New World has the moral backbone of a piece of wet bread.
Brave New World fares slightly better than the majority of its padded-out and mostly interminable brethren...
Captain America: Brave New World arrives saddled with a lot of baggage, and that's before the movie even starts.

An underbaked central narrative, bland expository dialogue, consistently drab visuals, poor characterisation and nondescript action scenes combine to create a conspiracy thriller lacking even a whiff of intrigue or paranoia.
...Captain America: A New World...is, quite simply, a tedious film on its own, and redundant in the grand scheme of things. [Full review in Spanish]

Because “The Boys” has done such an incredible job sending up superheroes, it’s hard for something like this to maneuver. Had Marvel corrupted someone in the Avengers, there might have been a need for someone else to rise to the challenge.

While the story is formulaic, I can appreciate the effort in character development. Anthony Mackie thrives in the title he's deservingly earned. Mackie provides depth and authenticity that humanizes his character.
If there is one HUGE problem Captain America: BNW cannot squash under flashy action scenes and clever quips, is the glaring and distracting CGI, which appears muddy and unfinished
Mackie, as Wilson, expresses the human vulnerability of Captain America, bringing a different kind of suspense to the fight scenes, and an interesting philosophical twist to the superhero series.

With solid performances, new characters, cameos in doses, and the occasional easter egg, the film has a certain narrative and visual austerity, making it much closer to the public than other, more lavish titles [Full Review in Spanish]
While Anthony Mackie’s Sam Wilson confidently wields the shield, the movie struggles to carry its weight, landing somewhere between an ambitious political thriller and a standard superhero outing.

Yet another installment in the MEH - C- U where Marvel has been consistently giving audience mediocre action films and gaslighting us to believe these are super hero stories. Sam never gets a chance to shine in this sludge of a messy drama.
Light and nimble at just under two hours, "Brave New World" maximizes its runtime with a series of thrilling action set pieces that Onah enacts with palpable freshness.
I found it absolutely impossible to get interested in it. The writing is at its very, very best functional.
Action scenes pop up frequently enough to keep the most fidgety teen engaged.
It's not worse than Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania, but still mediocre.

As a sequel to (The Incredible Hulk and The Eternals) it is effective enough, especially given the complaints surrounding both of them. Should they have done that in a Captain America movie? Probably not.
You can't assume the audience has seen all movies related to this one.
The film is positioned as a political thriller and is chock full of moving parts, zipping from plot point to plot point so quickly that it refuses to allow the viewer to become bored.

Brave New World is middling MCU , and the weakest of Captain’s solo outings, but still defies its messy production and over-stuffed plot to consistently entertain - especially when Mackie gets to shine.
It's solid.
It's an unfortunate revelation that this brave new post-"Endgame" world was not quite ready to give [Anthony Mackie] a sunny spot where he could shine.
The film works best as a platform for Mackie to emerge from Chris Evans' shadow, but doesn't successfully create a distinct enough personality.
Anthony Mackie salvages the Marvel film with a lackluster plot.

Unlike the title suggests there's little that feels brave or new as the studio attempts to stuff Wilson neatly into Cap's old image rather than build upon what makes him uniquely worthy of carrying the shield.
The film directed by Julius Onah is the worst it could have been: one that is neither good nor bad and that, quite simply, just exists.

The not-so-secret weapon this CAPTAIN AMERICA has going for it is Harrison Ford. Don’t believe the nay-sayers out there: Brave New World is a 21st century Tall Tale, and if it takes two viewings to take it all in, so be it
You can spot the pointless rewrites and pesky reshoots a mile off. Mackie (an affable hero) and Ford (a lively grump) are good value, as ever but the film around them is overcooked and underwhelming.
This is a pretty entertaining movie that raises the question of why soldiers, who swear and oath to the Constitution, should follow the orders of leaders who have broken that oath.

I’m not sure another director would have done any better with this messy, fragmented screenplay, but there are so few surprises or otherwise interesting moments that I can’t imagine audiences putting themselves through repeat viewings.

Ultimately, Captain America: Brave New World is the worst thing a Marvel movie can be – just ‘alright’...solid action and committed performances can’t cover up the superhero fatigue Hollywood is battling, where everything has been done before, and better.
It’s not actually a Captain America movie: It’s a Thunderbolt Ross movie.
When the most interesting side of the story flounders right out of the gate, the rest of “Brave New World” has to offer the same old stuff.

Captain America: Brave New World feels like the start of something new for the MCU. After the misfires of a few recent releases, there is a glimmer of hope that Marvel finally has a solid foundation for whatever the new phase will bring.

Captain America: Brave New World has little to do with the Aldous Huxley novel that gave it its name, nor does it deliver as incisive a social critique... It does, however, offer observations surprisingly congruent with a Christian ethic.
If Brave New World is a sign of things to come, then the MCU is in more trouble than we thought.
For the first time since “Endgame,” Marvel has given us a movie that truly feels like it lives up to the “Avengers” tradition.
It’s lighter fare than “Captain America: The Winter Soldier,” though there is still enough peril in the script to keep viewers fully invested.

To nobody’s surprise Captain America: Brave New World lacks any fresh ideas to contribute to the currently tiresome MCU. For one, it ends up confirming the franchises need for a serious break to think things over and come back with better ideas.

Neither cohesive enough or messy enough to really satisfy any of its objectives. Captain America is a strong enough character to get into his own mess, it’s incredibly disappointing that Sam Wilson and his film feel like the janitors of the MCU instead.
Brave New World bears the mark of a film made by feuding, status-obsessed middle managers.
If “Captain America: Brave New World” is flawed, it is not Mackie’s fault. His take on Captain America without the secret sauce is reminiscent of Tony Stark in “Iron Man 3” (2013).
Despite its evident production flaws, Julius Onah still manages to deliver moments of real entertainment, supported by a charismatic cast and well-crafted action sequences.
Anthony Mackie and Harrison Ford shine in the scene-setting Captain America: Brave New World, but they can’t lift the film out of the now-average MCU mire.
It feels as if Sam is merely the guest star in someone’s else story in this particular chapter of the MCU’s interwoven narrative.
Bloated misfire.
Alas, it’s only intermittently entertaining and still requires a lot of nerd homework to get all the references.
Is it worth seeing? Sure, it’s entertaining enough for a couple of hours, filled with some fun dialogue, exciting action, and a solid set of characters.
...a film that unexpectedly finds some wells of emotion, or pure humanity, in Harrison Ford's performance...[Full review in Spanish]

Brave New World is unconcerned with plumbing any of its latent politics, let alone exploring any fresh ground. Instead, the movie serves up another sloppily knocked-together bit of pseudo-entertainment.

If Brave New World isn’t the worst movie ever released under the Marvel banner, it might just be the dullest -- a humorless, grayed-out vision of contractual obligation featuring actors who look like they’d rather be anywhere else.
Mackie is a more than capable action hero and a wonderful comedic actor, though BNW makes too little use of the latter superpower.
Even with all its story problems and conflicted messaging, when it comes time for action, the film soars.
It’s a humourless drag of a picture, overreliant on clunky exposition and naive geopolitical posturing. Plus it’s ugly, with a greasy murkiness that looks as though the lens was smeared with lard.
Mackie instantly channels the requisite integrity and sturdy character of a worthy Captain America.
Brave New World takes center stage, but it never turns on the mic; lips move, but we don't hear anything at all.

The performances are strong, and the world-building is seeding potential for some cool future projects. All of this will obscure that it gets bogged down by choices that make the studio seem out of touch.

Captain America: Brave New World is the definition of mediocre — a movie so afraid to take a political stance that, while still being momentarily entertaining, it’s ultimately just a disposable sliver of popcorn entertainment.
What we also don't see anywhere is charisma or much less any character development. [Full review in Spanish]
I really appreciated that this movie focused on being its own story.

While not very exciting, it isn't terrible either, so it unfortunately ends up in the category of movies to watch while on a plane or if you have nothing else to do. If you are a Marvel fan... you should definitely give it a watch.
The film admirably coheres some of Marvel's vast continuity while delivering on the action and political thriller elements we expect from the franchise.

Brave New World has an aggressively OK feel to it that only accentuates its unchallenging narrative with themes left unexplored, arcs half-baked and action that is fine but uninspired. More than ever its clear the plan finished with Endgame.
Brave New World is neither a return to form for the MCU nor an unmitigated disaster. It is simply average, featuring numerous forgettable plot points that feel tacked together at the last second.
‘Brave New World’ will be an example of why comfort isn’t always the best medicine.

It fights against the notion that Captain America is political, while also including political imagery all the time. It’s at war trying to decide whether Captain America represents America or represents what America could and should be.
Captain America: Brave New World is a wasted opportunity.
It's clear Harrison Ford is having a total blast, but Anthony Mackie deserved a better script, the storylines were all over the place.

Captain America: Brave New World is a combination of The Winter Soldier, James Bond, and The Manchurian Candidate. Things start to feel out of place when the villain and Red Hulk show up. It's like a bunch of toys got mixed in with a political thriller.
It’s a toothless attempt at topicality. Because of that, there’s little that feels very brave and even less that struck me as new.

Superhero fatigue is here and it’s real. Look no further than Disney’s much-delayed addition to the MCU (Marvel Cinematic Universe), Captain America: Brave New World, as first and final proof of that proposition.
Overall, “Captain America: Brave New World” is a mid-level entry in the MCU that addresses several plot holes from previous films. It presents a reserved and cautious narrative.

This film over promised and under delivered. Incomplete storytelling, underdeveloped characters, meaningless setups and arc that felt rushed, but more importantly I felt it was a disservice to a character.

The movie also illustrates that Mackie’s Sam Wilson is a different Captain America than Steve. Unlike Steve, Sam is more in touch with his emotions as he grapples with the responsibility of wielding the shield and striving to improve the world.

Let’s get one thing out of the way: Sam Wilson is the correct character to take on the mantle of Captain America. Whatever issues Captain America: Brave New World has, they’re not Sam Wilson or actor Anthony Mackie’s fault.
While Captain America: Brave New World has some issues and could have used a stronger villain, the good moments are able to lift the movie above its flaws.
"... sanitized, risk free, and largely forgettable."

Better than I expected… There’s some enjoyable set pieces, but it’s very clunky and very goofy. Plays better as a Hulk sequel than a Cap movie. Mackie is fantastic, but wish he’d been given a meatier vehicle as his first theatrical Cap outing.

This iteration of Cap is a complete blank slate – devoid of moral standing or social cognizance. Because the character is made to see everything straight down the middle, we have no idea what he stands for.
'Captain America: Brave New World' is Marvel fatigue personified. It is a bland mess, dragged down by TV show tie-ins, humiliating visual effects and a baffling script written by nine people.

With a strong storyline that takes things back to basics, a stellar central performance from Mackie and a solid message behind it, Captain America: Brave New World manages to both entertain and impress.
It’s all pretty silly, of course, but it’s not punishingly overlong, and director Julius Onah stages an amusing finale involving the Red Hulk rampaging among the cherry blossoms in D.C.

This is a horrible entry in the Marvel universe. There is so much exposition...explanation after explanation and you just get bored with it. I disliked this movie so much I didn't bother to see the end credit scene.
An overstuffed espionage thriller... falls short of greatness, perfectly watchable but too focused on what-comes-next rather than happening-right-now in an eerily Iron Man 2 kind of way.

It carries some strong underpinnings of Malcolm Spellman's great The Falcon and The Winter Solider but ultimately falters. The film's casting and characterizations are generally strong. However, the story is chopped and end up just being a middling story.

Brave New World is a fine but often frustrating geopolitical affair. Mackie, Ramirez & Lumbly all share an excellent chemistry but they’re unfortunately forced to play second fiddle in an overstuffed sequel to The Incredible Hulk and Eternals.
A best of collection of Marvel's afterthoughts.
In keeping with the MCU’s increasing insularity, the vast conspiracy is mostly just a collection of loose ends from other Marvel projects that doesn’t add up to much.

While the performances by Ford, Mackie, and Ramirez are solid, the film as a whole struggles with moments of blandness and does not successfully create a distinct enough personality for the new Captain America.

Very much a return to form for Marvel Studios’ long-term storytelling. The Multiverse Saga hasn’t been as smooth as The Infinity Saga, but this felt like the connective foundation desperately needed to get MCU fans excited about the future of the brand.
There's a lot of world building that takes place in this film, but...it actually holds up as a single installment on its own.
“Brave New World” includes some interesting political references but they are oblique enough to avoid certain volatile current affairs.
Certainly, the advent of the Disney/Marvel teams connecting for streaming content that only the most rabid MCU fans might have seen leaves this one a bit messy around the plot edges.

As with other Captain America content, this film attempts a taut political thriller. It works for the most part, though there’s some clunky dialogue and it bends over backwards to avoid being too political.
If you are permanently glued to everything Marvel Studios makes, it is an enjoyable two hours of entertainment – but that, honestly, is about it

Captain America feels like a supporting character in his own movie. What should be a thrilling comic book blockbuster instead plays out like a condensed, clunky version of an anticlimactic, made-for-Disney+ series.
The screenplay from Rob Edwards and the work from the writing teams of Malcolm Spellman & Dalan Musson and Onah & Peter Glanz have made a mess of what made Marvel of old engaging.
It represents the MCU on autopilot, and while that means everything runs smoothly, it never goes anywhere particularly interesting.
Captain America: Brave New World was a fine movie. Serviceable. . . it fell within the expected parameters.
Somewhere, buried beneath all this plot, is an interesting movie struggling to breathe.

Despite its convoluted plot and occasional pacing issues, Brave New World delivers thrilling aerial battles and hand-to-hand combats, strong performances, and enough spectacle to entertain superhero fans.
As for Feige, whose name means cowardly in German, he will need to screw his courage and return with something bolder if the coming Phase Six of Marvel is truly going to offer a Brave New World.

It feels closer to a compacted season of "Falcon and the Winter Soldier" than "Captain America: The Winter Soldier," but the more experienced actors elevate the material with their own superpower: Electrifying charisma. [Full Review in Spanish]

For those expecting something more substantial, the film feels like leftovers—reheated and lacking real depth. The only thing this comic book film assembles is boredom, a humdrum Marvel experience if there ever was one.
...Captain America: Brave New World isn't able to match up to the expectations nor the legacy driven ideas of the MCU's past.
A solid, if unspectacular, superhero movie with a couple of decent action sequences and better CGI than other recent MCU films.
Captain America: Brave New World finds Marvel with its head up its own posterior.
Captain America: Brave New World turns the titular character into a political spectator, not an active participant.
Talk of the Avengers reassembling recalls happier days, but Marvel hasn’t yet found the serum to rejuvenate its exhausted universe.
Brave New World isn’t the worst offender but it’s a reminder that the formulas upon which the MCU was built are no longer effective. An adjustment is needed but it doesn’t come here.
...the film is extremely entertaining, though this doesn't change the fact that the credited screenwriters still relied on several plot points that are extremely predictable. [Full review in Spanish]
Brave New World is a typical Marvel movie, but also not...It’s a rock-solid Marvel movie that’s lots of fun, while not afraid to be a bit different.

We've had various iterations of the superhero movie, and here's the political thriller version -- though sometimes lacking in thrills. The second half's exciting action overcomes an overly talkie first half.
It was neither brave nor new.
...there is no attractive hero,... there are no villains of substance...and the supporting characters are neither likeable, funny, nor charming. [Full review in Spanish]
Captain America: Brave New World and its back-to-basics approach feels like the reset that the superfranchise could use.

To those familiar with The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, this continuation may satisfy. However, to the uninitiated, Captain America: Brave New World feels like the boring middle portion of a much longer story.

As excellent as Evans was as Cap, Mackie’s shown equal skill in crafting his own version of what that character should mean – in his case, weathering the pressures and politics of being a national symbol and being as adept with his words as his fists.
It is a sad reflection on the quality of our current political leadership that the fictional President Red Hulk passes this test while our real-life leaders consistently fail it.
The sorry scribblers seem to be marking time for a bigger and better Marvel gathering to come, but they could have tried harder to hide their boredom.
The MCU is event cinema, and the bigger it gets, the more an audience expects in return. Two decades in, a low-rent Iron Man with wings just doesn't cut it.
Despite some known production issues and challenges, Captain America gave us a strong story anchored by solid performances from Anthony Mackie and Carl Lumbly.

Carl Lumbly and Anthony Mackie did their best to elevate what turned out to be a pretty run of the mill Marvel film into something more. Their performances alone make this a solid viewing experience but I just wish the film had a clearer focus.
This 35th Marvel Studios film is blessedly short, brings some long threads of storyline to a close and hints at a few new ones, and is mildly enjoyable.

Despite a budget of close to 200 million, the MCU has rarely felt smaller than Brave New World, which often feels like an episode of The West Wing without any of the quippy writing or coherent plot progression.

Fueled by nostalgia and nationalism, Captain America: Brave New World is an alienating disgrace that actively disrespects its lead for a directionless, if not the poorest, attempt for the MCU to cling onto its own relevancy.

I can't believe at one time I complained about these Marvel movies having too many superheroes per movie because Brave New World feels empty with only one, especially one that could more easily die in any fight he's in.

Anthony Mackie fights hard with his vibranium wings, but the Marvel magic didn’t take flight for this one. Marvel and Disney are still looking for that Brave New World. Maybe in the next one, it will magically appear.
Problems with this movie start with the odd choice to base the plot of “Brave New World” on two little-known and lower-performing MCU installments.
As another stepping stone for whatever the MCU is leading up to with Avengers: Doomsday next year, Brave New World is a decent entry in the post-Endgame canon.

Captain America: Brave New World offers some decent action and a fresh lead in Anthony Mackie’s charismatic Sam Wilson, but a messy plot – much of it spoiled by the film’s own marketing – and rushed characterisation leave it well below the MCU’s standard.
This is a film that should have been much more, no matter what the current political moment looked like, but instead it's left scrambling for purpose, unsure of what to stand for if anything at all.
... a glaringly average MCU installment that does nothing to bring back the big event feel that every MCU movie once had.
While Brave New World may not be a cinematic feast, it’s a satisfying amuse-bouche that whet my appetite for the next phase of the MCU.
This new Captain America isn’t a super­soldier, so his fists don’t pack the same mighty punch. But he can surely bludgeon both friends and foes with self-righteous platitudes.
Despite Mackie and Ford’s best efforts, a disappointing and lacklustre filler shouldn’t be the feeling associated with Captain America, and yet, this star-spangled film is devoid of care and heart.
The lie in the title “Captain America: Brave New World” can be found in the fourth word. There’s nothing new about this chapter.

In contrast, “Brave New World” feels stuck, spending more time tying up loose ends from films like “The Incredible Hulk” and “Eternals” than giving Sam Wilson now Captain America – anything meaningful to fight for.

While it was admittedly idiotic of me to go looking for ideas in a $180 million Disney movie, for that price one should expect at least a modicum of craft. And on that level ‘Brave New World’ is a catastrophe.

Brave New World has its eyes set high in the skies but it ends up doubting itself by revisiting ghosts of the MCU. The result is a lacklustre instalment that fails to pull the universe out of its funk.
It's doubtful that Captain America: Brave New World will be anyone's favorite Captain America movie, but it does enough to still keep audiences invested in the MCU.
It's a solid entry into the MCU.

It’s too much to saddle his stand-alone film with this much exposition, and yet, Mackie and Onah bear it with as much grace as they can… a decent political thriller with something culturally resonant to say that exceeds mere comic-book particulars.

If “Brave New World” isn’t an event film, at least it’s competently executed, without resorting to played-out gimmickry such as skipping across the multiverse. And it gives the audience plenty of analogues for real-world problems.
A new era for Anthony Mackie’s Sam Wilson begins with Captain America: Brave New World, and while he is worthy of the shield, the rest of the film doesn’t live up to the series standard.
Less than super...

The film comes together as a somewhat watchable Marvel superhero event, led by a strong, anchoring performance by Anthony Mackie. Brave New World is not a complete disaster but fails to reach the heights of the previous films it wants to emulate.

When approaching a comic book movie, I don't expect Shakespeare, as roots are pulp fiction! So the latest Cap joint is in the Marvel zeitgeist, managed to predict correctly our current "Hulk Smash" presidency, and was a decent comic book story. SMASH!
Despite committed performances from Mackie and Ford, this one is neither daring nor fresh. With a lackluster villain and drab visuals, overall it's an underwhelming MCU entry.
It’s a model of economical storytelling, not using too many characters or getting too complex
In all likelihood, Captain America: Brave New World, like The Incredible Hulk, is destined to be equally maligned and memory-holed.

Anthony Mackie is the driving force behind a good old time at the movies that reminded me of a school night at the cinema with my dad when I was a kid. No world-building, just an action adventure that aims to please and ease the mind.
Thankfully even at 82, Ford is able to rescue this with his considerable charisma.

Though the plot isn’t massively complex, it’s dense, involving multiple references to previous Marvel shows, while also shoehorning in a series of last-minute plot twists... But hey, if you’re not into that – look! A giant Red Hulk!

Elevated by Anthony Mackie's everyman's Captain America and Harrison Ford's on-screen charisma and work as President Ross, Brave New World results in a fun, middle of the pack MCU outing. Overall, okay enough. [Full review in Spanish]
It feels destined that Brave New World will fade away into the void of MCU projects without much thought or attention. A deserved fate for a film so unwilling to craft something new or meaningful.
In spite of fine cast, Captain America: Brave New World is more Marvel content. Bring on Victor Von Doom.
...the movie flirts with topicality as it tries to keep the Marvel torch burning. Yes, the flame sometimes sputters, but like Mackie, Brave New World ultimately holds its own.

While it definitely has its flaws, Brave New World is still an explosive, exciting, and powerful start to Avengers 2.0 Sam once again picks up the shield with some enhancements and proves himself to be worthy of the shield and a seat at the table.
...[Captain America: Brave New World] is pleasant, bearable, has no jumps between parallel universes, is more linear and understandable. [Full review in Spanish]

A tossed salad of yearning for yet another “phase” that will get the Avengers band and brand back together again... The action scenes are plentiful, the editing incomprehensible—oh for the glory days of... scalpel-like onslaughts of clockwork Bayhem.
Brave New World isn’t just a grand missed opportunity, but is simply more of the same soulless, crass, and entirely neutered product for which the MCU project has slowly but surely become known.
If this were the final test to see if Mackie could shoulder the responsibility of being Captain America, then he would have more than earned his wings.
With the politically incoherent, creatively inert and just plain insulting sequel Captain America: Brave New World, the MCU brain trust led by uber-producer Kevin Feige has truly flatlined.
Messy and unsatisfying, Anthony Mackie is worthy of the shield but deserves so much better in his first big-screen outing as Cap.
...Brave New World works as a fairly effective entertainment, largely thanks to the irresistible presence of [Harrison] Ford. [Full review in Spanish]
For his part, Mackie is charismatic and has star power, though he still feels somewhat timid in the role, and he lacks the character moments to truly shine.

For the MCU to make it back to their previous standing atop the blockbuster landscape, they’re going to have to deliver much more interesting characters and stories than are present in Captain America: Brave New World.
Thankfully, the script never bogs down in explanations beyond short bursts of gobbledegook, which helps director Onah focus on the characters and their messy motivations and inter-relationships.
Another tedious slog in the Marvel superhero sausage factory....  Even the most devoted fans will find it a letdown.
Captain America: Brave New World showcases technical strengths, but flaws in CGI and execution keep it from reaching its full potential.
The movie’s more interested in fan service and protecting corporate IP then in telling that story, or any story.
The movie wouldn't feel human at all, really, if not for the convincing emotion bond established between Mackie and Carl Lumbly as Isaiah.
As the kind of action-fantasy spectacular expected from Marvel, Brave New World is a non-starter. Often it feels closer to a TV procedural...
The pleasures offered in “Captain America: Brave New World” are neither grand nor groundbreaking, but they’re consistent and earned.
The latest Captain America installment is a competent, if unremarkable, entry that neatly ties up a few lingering storylines without making a significant impact on the larger MCU.

The fight sequences are meditative, the grave-whisper acting belongs in a coming-attraction trailer from 1996 and, yet again, the viewer needs to have watched a TV series and at least two movies to fully grasp what’s happening.
With its cheap action and garish visuals, it’s then that we enter yet another genre altogether: action-figure commercial.
This is a Temu knock-off compared to Winter Soldier.

I wasn't bored watching it, and that's the least I ask for from any movie, especially from a superhero flick. But it shouldn't be that way, especially with a brand that has given us so many exciting moments in cinema. [Full review in Spanis]
You get a good forty minutes of “Smash!…Boom!…Pow!” sprinkled around two hours of allusions to a geopolitical landscape that the film is ultimately uninterested in or unwilling to explore.
This "oops, all understudies!" take on The Avengers continues the MCU's march to cultural irrelevancy.
Instead of feeling like the big, splashy debut of a new era for the MCU, Brave New World feels like the subpar sequel to a better movie that doesn’t actually exist.

...the film is reminiscent of the franchise's most forgettable products, such as Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania (2023) or Black Widow (2021): films made on autopilot, where the functional replaces the inspirational. [Full review in Spanish]
Captain America: Brave New World attempts to recapture that lost glow but only manages to muster a flickering light.

The...thoughtful treatment of Blackness and solid...action thriller elements are worth something, but they don't outweigh the sense that the film is meant to pacify any potentially galvanizing political feeling in American audiences.
Captain America: Brave New World is not breaking any new ground but it’s throwback feel is a reminder that less can be more for Marvel when they have a great cast and simple story to tell.
With a plot that is artificially complicated, forgettable characters and the intention to set the stage for events that will occur later, the film falters throughout. [Full Review in Spanish]
It is an action-packed journey with plenty of political espionage that lays an excellent foundation for higher-stakes stories in the future. The film isn’t a masterpiece, but doesn’t need to be.

Mackie is not to blame and we know he is deservedly going to be entrenched as Captain America for the upcoming Avengers projects. Still, it leaves his first solo outing in the forgettable middle tier of MCU project rankings.
Captain America: Brave New World is nothing extravagant, but that's what makes it feel different among its more recent peers...

What could have very well been developed as an interesting thriller, trying to at least be on the level of "The Winter Soldier", has instead ended up becoming a chaotic, irregular, visually ugly and at times tedious experience. [Full review in Spanish].
Mackie and Ford bring their A-game, but Marvel movies shouldn't be this dull.

As a turn-your-brain-off, techno action movie, it succeeds well enough. As a Marvel movie that connects with other Marvel movies in any meaningful way or charts a new direction, it’s little more than a space-filler.
For those willing to buy in, the film has a sense of fun whilst wrangling with some real world issues such as the distribution of resources and what it means to be a Black man in a flag suit.

Captain America: Brave New World has entertaining aerial scenes and, in the Red Hulk, a role that allows Harrison Ford, the best angry man in movies, to let his freak flag fly but it doesn’t have the epic feel of other MCU movies.
